knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand MPCC Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal directional stationarity over the Bouligand tangent cone to the MPCC feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\) be the feasible set of the continuously differentiable MPCC with constraints \(g(x)\leq0\), \(h(x)=0\), \(G(x)\geq0\), \(H(x)\geq0\), and \(G_i(x)H_i(x)=0\) for every complementarity index \(i\). At a feasible point \(\bar x\), define the Bouligand tangent cone by
\[T_\Omega(\bar x)=\left\{d:\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists d_k\to d\text{ with }\bar x+t_kd_k\in\Omega\text{ for every }k\right\}.\]
The point \(\bar x\) is Bouligand MPCC-stationary if
\[\nabla f(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d\geq0\qquad\text{for every }d\in T_\Omega(\bar x).\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d\geq0\) for every \(d\in T_\Omega(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strong–Bouligand Coincidence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of strong multiplier stationarity and primal Bouligand stationarity under MPCC-LICQ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a feasible point \(\bar x\), suppose MPCC-LICQ holds: the gradients of all equalities, active ordinary inequalities, \(G_i\) for \(i\in I^{0+}\cup I^{00}\), and \(H_i\) for \(i\in I^{+0}\cup I^{00}\) are linearly independent. Then \(\bar x\) is Bouligand MPCC-stationary if and only if it is strongly MPCC-stationary. Under this hypothesis the multiplier system is unique, and polarity of the MPCC linearized cone forces the biactive multipliers to satisfy \(\nu_i\geq0\) and \(\xi_i\geq0\). Thus the primal directional certificate and the strong multiplier certificate describe the same stationary points in the MPCC-LICQ regime.

MPCC-LICQ holds at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strong–Bouligand Separation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate complementarity mapping separates primal Bouligand stationarity from strong multiplier stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the one-dimensional MPCC minimizing \(f(x)=x\) subject to \(G(x)=x^2\geq0\), \(H(x)=x^2\geq0\), and \(G(x)H(x)=0\). Its feasible set is the singleton \(\{0\}\); hence its tangent cone at \(0\) is \(\{0\}\), and \(0\) is Bouligand-stationary. However, \(G'(0)=H'(0)=0\), so every strong-stationarity multiplier equation reduces to
\[0=f'(0)-\nu G'(0)-\xi H'(0)=1,\]
which is impossible. Thus Bouligand stationarity need not imply strong stationarity when the complementarity gradients are degenerate and an MPCC constraint qualification fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With vanishing complementarity gradients, an isolated feasible point is Bouligand-stationary although no strong multiplier equation can hold.
assumptions_latex: The complementarity convention is \(G\geq0\), \(H\geq0\), and \(GH=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=0\) is Bouligand-stationary but not strongly stationary.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility–Stationarity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate tolerances prevent one residual scale from concealing poor feasibility or poor criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_f(x)\geq0\) measure constraint violation and \(r_s(x)\geq0\) measure stationarity. An \((\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_s)\)-certificate requires \(r_f(x)\leq\varepsilon_f\) and \(r_s(x)\leq\varepsilon_s\). For weights \(a,b>0\), the scalar bound \(a r_f(x)+b r_s(x)\leq\varepsilon\) implies only \(r_f(x)\leq\varepsilon/a\) and \(r_s(x)\leq\varepsilon/b\). Conversely, the two componentwise bounds imply \(a r_f(x)+b r_s(x)\leq a\varepsilon_f+b\varepsilon_s\). Thus changing weights changes the certified tradeoff unless an additional error-bound relation links the residuals.

assumptions_latex: \(r_f,r_s\) are nonnegative residual functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a r_f+b r_s\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow(r_f\leq\varepsilon/a,\ r_s\leq\varepsilon/b)\), while componentwise bounds imply the corresponding weighted bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weakly convex finite-dimensional stationarity measured by the gradient of a differentiable Moreau envelope.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-to-Near-Point Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Envelope criticality transfers to limiting-subdifferential criticality at the associated nearby proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, let \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), and set \(y=P_\lambda(x)\). Proximal optimality and weak convexity give \(v=\lambda^{-1}(x-y)=\nabla f_\lambda(x)\in\partial f(y)\). Consequently, if \(\|\nabla f_\lambda(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\), then \(\|x-y\|\leq\lambda\varepsilon\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(y))\leq\varepsilon\). Thus envelope stationarity at \(x\) certifies ordinary limiting-subdifferential stationarity at a quantitatively nearby point \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small envelope gradient produces a proximal point within λε whose limiting subdifferential contains a vector of norm at most ε.

\(0<\lambda<1/\rho\) and \(y=P_\lambda(x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone-inclusion residual obtained by evaluating the resolvent of a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space and let \(\lambda>0\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximal monotone, let \(\lambda>0\), and define the fixed-point residual \(F_{\lambda A}(x)=x-J_{\lambda A}x\). children.top_down_role: Stationarity-to-global-optimality routes under generalized pseudoconvexity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz on an open neighborhood of \(C\).
For all \(x,y\in C\), \(f^{\circ}(x;y-x)\ge0\) implies \(f(y)\ge f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)\), then \(f(y)\ge f(\bar x)\) for every \(y\in C\); hence \(\bar x\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-pseudoconvex sufficiency for unconstrained stationarity on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar x\in C\) satisfy \(0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)\). By the support representation of the Clarke derivative, \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;y-\bar x)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(\bar x)}\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Clarke pseudoconvexity, expressed by the second assumption, therefore gives \(f(y)\ge f(\bar x)\) for all \(y\in C\). Thus Clarke stationarity is a sufficient certificate of global optimality under this generalized-pseudoconvex structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Clarke-pseudoconvex locally Lipschitz function, every Clarke-stationary point is a global minimizer on the convex domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Pseudoconvex Optimality Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is plausible for the explicitly stated Clarke-pseudoconvex implication, but no source identifies this generalized-pseudoconvex variant or supports the exact hypotheses. The statement also contains proof-style reasoning that must be removed once the sourced theorem formulation is fixed.

children.title: Generalized-Quasiconvex Optimality Tests
children.top_down_role: Directional and level-set tests under generalized quasiconvexity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized directional quasiconvexity test is \(f(y)\le f(x)\Rightarrow f^{\circ}(x;y-x)\le0\) for all \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke directional formulation tied to lower level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally Lipschitz function satisfies the Clarke directional quasiconvexity test on \(C\) when, for every \(x\in C\), \[y\in L_f(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^{\circ}(x;y-x)\le0\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Equivalently, every direction from \(x\) toward a point in its lower level set has nonpositive Clarke generalized directional derivative. This is a structural test; unlike pseudoconvexity, it does not by itself make the inclusion \(0\in\partial_C f(x)\) sufficient for global minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional quasiconvexity requires every direction toward a no-higher objective value to have nonpositive Clarke directional derivative; this alone does not make stationarity sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Quasiconvex Optimality Tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for treating the displayed Clarke directional implication as the intended generalized-quasiconvex condition. Clarke, Dini, and other directional formulations are not interchangeable without regularity assumptions, so the exact mathematical variant cannot be confirmed.

children.title: Generalized-Convexity Sufficiency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure of stationarity-based sufficiency when the required generalized-convex structure is absent.

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=x^3\) on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(0\in\partial_C f(0)\), the point \(0\) is not a minimizer; hence stationarity is insufficient without an appropriate generalized-pseudoconvex assumption.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth scalar counterexample; quasiconvexity alone does not upgrade stationarity to optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is smooth, increasing, and therefore quasiconvex, while \(\partial_C f(0)=\{0\}\). Nevertheless, for every \(y<0\), \(f(y)<f(0)=0\), so zero is not a local or global minimizer. Moreover, taking \(x=0\) and \(y=-1\) gives \(f'(0)(y-x)=0\) but \(f(y)<f(x)\), violating the pseudoconvex implication. Thus stationarity-based global sufficiency fails when the stronger generalized-convex structure is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasiconvex function x cubed is stationary at zero but decreases to its left, showing that quasiconvexity alone does not make stationarity sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Convexity Sufficiency Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The x-cubed example is mathematically correct and well matched to the sufficiency-boundary leaf, but the record supplies neither an evidence reference nor an explicit standard-field rationale. Source support is therefore required under the evidence contract.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Analytical-Constraint Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An ε-Clarke–KKT certificate for locally Lipschitz inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz, and let \(x\) satisfy \(g_i(x)\leq0\). For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), an \(\varepsilon\)-relaxed analytical-constraint certificate consists of multipliers \(\lambda_i\geq0\), subgradients \(v_0\in\partial_C f(x)\), and \(v_i\in\partial_C g_i(x)\) such that
\[\left\|v_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i v_i\right\|\leq\varepsilon,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i|g_i(x)|\leq\varepsilon.\]
It certifies approximate Clarke stationarity and approximate complementarity; by itself it does not certify local or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers and Clarke subgradients certify relaxed constrained stationarity when the Lagrangian residual and total complementarity error are at most ε.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
\(g_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i\partial_C g_i(x))\leq\varepsilon\) with approximate complementarity.

children.top_down_role: Quasidifferential criticality and optimality for unconstrained problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Quasidifferential Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessary condition for a finite-dimensional quasidifferentiable local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\) and has quasidifferential \([A,B]\), where \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty compact convex sets and
\[f'(\bar x;d)=\max_{a\in A}\langle a,d\rangle+\min_{b\in B}\langle b,d\rangle.\]
If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer, then \(f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\). Equivalently,
\[-B\subseteq A.\]
This inclusion is quasidifferential stationarity and is generally necessary, not sufficient, for local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an unconstrained quasidifferentiable local minimum, every directional derivative is nonnegative, equivalently the negative upper quasidifferential lies inside the lower one.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
\(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty compact convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\) for all \(d\), equivalently \(-B\subseteq A\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The necessary condition and inclusion equivalence are mathematically consistent under the displayed quasidifferential convention, and the condition kind fits the leaf. No inspectable source supports that convention or result.

children.title: Quasidifferential Descent Certificates
children.top_down_role: Separation between quasidifferential stationarity and explicit descent regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasidifferential Descent Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directly verifiable strict-descent certificate from quasidifferential components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \([A,B]\) represent the quasidifferential of \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) at \(x\). A pair \((b,d)\in B\times\mathbb R^n\) is a strict quasidifferential descent certificate if
\[\max_{a\in A}\langle a,d\rangle+\langle b,d\rangle<0.\]
Because
\[f'(x;d)=\max_{a\in A}\langle a,d\rangle+\min_{u\in B}\langle u,d\rangle,\]
the displayed inequality implies \(f'(x;d)<0\). In particular, if some \(b\in B\) satisfies \(-b\notin A\), strong separation supplies such a direction \(d\), so \(x\) cannot be a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper component and a direction whose combined support value is negative certify strict directional descent and rule out local minimality.
assumptions_latex: \([A,B]\) is a quasidifferential of \(f\) at \(x\).
\(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)<0\), hence \(x\) is not a local minimizer.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed pair is a valid strict-descent certificate under the displayed quasidifferential convention, and the content kind fits the leaf. An authoritative locator is required to establish the convention and separation-based conclusion.

children.title: Constrained Quasidifferential Conditions
children.top_down_role: Geometric and multiplier certificates for quasidifferentiable constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Quasidifferential Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A primal directional condition for quasidifferentiable inequality-constrained problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\leq0\), where \(f,g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are Hadamard directionally differentiable at a feasible point \(\bar x\) and their directional derivatives admit quasidifferential representations. Let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer, there is no direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying simultaneously
\[f'(\bar x;d)<0,\qquad g_i'(\bar x;d)<0\quad\text{for every }i\in I(\bar x).\]
Thus every strict first-order feasible direction obeys \(f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\). Multiplier reformulations require an additional quasidifferential constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained local minimum admits no direction that strictly decreases both the objective and every active quasidifferentiable constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is feasible and \(f,g_i\) are Hadamard directionally differentiable there.
Each directional derivative has a finite-dimensional quasidifferential representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_i'(\bar x;d)<0\) for all \(i\in I(\bar x)\) implies \(f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict directional exclusion is plausible for the stated finite-dimensional Hadamard setting and is correctly distinguished from multiplier conditions, but no source verifies the exact constrained quasidifferential formulation or its hypotheses.

children.title: Epsilon-Quasidifferential Optimality
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-based quasidifferential criticality and optimality conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Quasidifferential Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-tolerant quasidifferential stationarity in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \([A,B]\) be a quasidifferential of \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) at \(x\), with \(A,B\) nonempty compact convex, and let \(\varepsilon\geq0\). The point \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-quasidifferentially stationary when
\[-B\subseteq A+\varepsilon\mathbb B.\]
Equivalently, its directional derivative satisfies
\[f'(x;d)\geq-\varepsilon\|d\|\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n.\]
For \(\varepsilon=0\) this reduces to exact quasidifferential stationarity. For positive tolerance it excludes directions having normalized first-order decrease greater than \(\varepsilon\), but it does not alone guarantee approximate objective optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon-stationarity means the negative upper quasidifferential lies within ε of the lower component, equivalently no unit direction decreases faster than ε.
assumptions_latex: \([A,B]\) is a quasidifferential of \(f\) at \(x\).
\(A,B\) are nonempty compact convex sets and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-B\subseteq A+\varepsilon\mathbb B\), equivalently \(f'(x;d)\geq-\varepsilon\|d\|\) for every \(d\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set inclusion and directional inequality are equivalent under the displayed Euclidean quasidifferential convention, and condition is the appropriate kind. The epsilon convention lacks authoritative support.

children.title: Codifferential Stationarity

knowledge_statements.title: Codifferential Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity expressed through normalized lower and upper codifferential slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be codifferentiable at \(x\), with lower and upper codifferentials \(\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\), normalized by
\[\max_{(a,v)\in\underline d f(x)}a=0,\qquad \min_{(b,w)\in\overline d f(x)}b=0.\]
Define \(A_0=\{v:(0,v)\in\underline d f(x)\}\) and \(B_0=\{w:(0,w)\in\overline d f(x)\}\). If \(x\) is an unconstrained local minimizer, then
\[-B_0\subseteq A_0.\]
Equivalently, every upper zero-slice vector \(w\) is balanced by a lower zero-slice vector \(-w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a codifferentiable local minimum, every vector in the normalized upper zero slice has its negative in the lower zero slice.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is codifferentiable at \(x\).
The lower and upper codifferentials are nonempty compact convex sets with the displayed normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-B_0\subseteq A_0\).

notation.meaning: zero-scalar slices of the two codifferentials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationarity condition fits the leaf, but its validity depends on the precise codifferential normalization and on whether the directional derivative is represented by the stated zero slices. Those conventions require a specific source.

children.title: Codifferential Descent Conditions

knowledge_statements.title: Codifferential Descent Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strict-descent test using normalized codifferential zero slices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the normalized codifferential notation \(A_0,B_0\), a pair \((w,d)\in B_0\times\mathbb R^n\) is a codifferential descent certificate if
\[\max_{v\in A_0}\langle v,d\rangle+\langle w,d\rangle<0.\]
The codifferential directional expansion then yields
\[f'(x;d)\leq\max_{v\in A_0}\langle v,d\rangle+\langle w,d\rangle<0,\]
so \(d\) is a strict descent direction. In particular, the failure \(-B_0\subseteq A_0\) produces such a certificate by strong separation and rules out local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-slice upper vector and separating direction certify negative directional derivative, thereby ruling out local minimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is codifferentiable at \(x\) with normalized compact convex codifferentials.
\(A_0\) and \(B_0\) are the corresponding zero-scalar slices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)<0\), hence \(x\) is not a local minimizer.

notation.meaning: normalized lower and upper zero slices

children.title: Stationarity Error-Bound Interface
children.top_down_role: Residual control of distance to stationary or solution sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Error-Bound Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric subregularity converts a stationarity residual into distance from the stationary set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Using the limiting subdifferential \(\partial f\) and limiting normal cone \(N_C\), define \(M(x)=\partial f(x)+N_C(x)\). Suppose \(0\in M(\bar x)\) and \(M\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\): there exist \(\kappa,\rho>0\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,M^{-1}(0)\bigr)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}\bigl(0,M(x)\bigr)\qquad\text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<\rho.\]
Writing \(S=M^{-1}(0)\) and \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))\), this gives the local stationarity error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity of the limiting-subdifferential stationarity mapping bounds local distance to the stationary set by a constant times the stationarity residual.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is closed and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(M(x)=\partial f(x)+N_C(x)\) uses the limiting subdifferential and limiting normal cone.
\(0\in M(\bar x)\) and \(M\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) whenever \(x\) is sufficiently near \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the closed set C

children.title: Sharpness-Growth Certificate Interface

children.title: Sharp-Minimum Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local structures where objective separation gives stationarity certificates stronger solution meaning.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp-Minimum Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear objective growth away from a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The point \(\bar x\) is a local sharp minimizer with modulus \(\alpha>0\) if there exists \(\rho>0\) such that
\[f(x)\geq f(\bar x)+\alpha\|x-\bar x\|\qquad\text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<\rho.\]
For a non-singleton local solution set \(S\), the setwise version replaces \(\|x-\bar x\|\) by \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) and \(f(\bar x)\) by the common local minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sharp minimum has objective value growing at least linearly with distance from the minimizer or local solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
\(\alpha>0\) and \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f(\bar x)\geq\alpha\|x-\bar x\|\) locally.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise definition is standard and the definition kind fits the leaf, but neither it nor the briefly stated setwise variant has an authoritative locator.

children.title: Objective-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Growth structures supporting quantitative interpretation of stationarity residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type local growth relative to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), and write \(f^*=\inf f\). For \(q\geq1\), the function has local growth of order \(q\) around \(\bar x\in S\) if there exist \(\alpha,ho>0\) such that
\[f(x)-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^q\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb B_\rho(\bar x).\]
The cases \(q=1\) and \(q=2\) are respectively sharp and quadratic growth. The definition controls objective gap from below but does not by itself impose a stationarity error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-q growth lower-bounds the objective gap by a positive multiple of the qth power of distance to the solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\) and \(\bar x\in S\).
\(q\geq1\) and \(\alpha,\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^q\) locally around \(\bar x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The power-growth definition is internally coherent and matches the leaf. A source is required because conventions differ concerning local versus global solution sets and normalization of quadratic growth.

children.title: Residual Error-Bound Consequences
children.top_down_role: Distance-to-solution consequences available when suitable growth structure is present.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error-Bound Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex objective growth yields quantitative lower bounds on subgradient residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with nonempty minimizer set \(S\). Suppose that near \(S\),
\[f(x)-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^q\]
for some \(\alpha>0\) and \(q\geq1\). With \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\), every nearby \(x\notin S\) satisfies
\[r(x)\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^{q-1}.\]
Consequently, if \(q>1\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq(r(x)/\alpha)^{1/(q-1)}\); if \(q=1\), every nonoptimal nearby point has \(r(x)\geq\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, order-q growth forces the subgradient residual to dominate distance raised to q−1, producing a Hölder error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
Local order-\(q\) growth holds with \(q\geq1\) and modulus \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(x)\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^{q-1}\) locally outside \(S\).

notation.meaning: minimum norm of a convex subgradient at \(x\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated finite-dimensional convex assumptions, the residual lower bound and its Hölder consequence are consistent, and property is the correct content kind. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Growth Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Flat or degenerate regimes where small residuals lack strong solution implications.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth Degeneracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A flat polynomial minimum separating Hölder from Lipschitz residual error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x)=x^4\). Its unique minimizer and stationary point is \(0\), while
\[f(x)-f(0)=|x|^4,\qquad r(x)=|f'(x)|=4|x|^3.\]
Thus neither sharp growth nor quadratic growth holds at \(0\). Moreover, no constants \(\kappa,\rho>0\) can satisfy \(|x|\leq\kappa r(x)\) for all \(|x|<\rho\). The exact residual-distance relation is instead
\[|x|=\left(r(x)/4\right)^{1/3}.\]
Hence higher-order flatness permits small stationarity residuals without a local Lipschitz error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function x⁴ has a unique minimum but only a cubic residual, so its residual controls distance Hölderly rather than Lipschitzly.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=x^4\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No local bound \(|x|\leq\kappa r(x)\) holds, although \(|x|=(r(x)/4)^{1/3}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The x-to-the-fourth example correctly separates Hölder residual control from a Lipschitz error bound, and failure_boundary is the exact role for this leaf. The record nevertheless supplies neither cited evidence nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Small Residual Far from Solutions
children.top_down_role: Failure of residual-to-distance control without an appropriate error bound.

assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon<1\), with \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
Stationarity is measured by \(r_\varepsilon(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f_\varepsilon(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), \(r_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)\to0\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x_\varepsilon,S_\varepsilon)\to\infty\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth convex scaling counterexample to any uniform residual-to-distance implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), let \(f_\varepsilon:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(f_\varepsilon(x)=\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}x^2\). Its unique stationary solution is \(S_\varepsilon=\{0\}\), and \(\partial f_\varepsilon(x)=\{\varepsilon x\}\). At \(x_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\), \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon))=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow0,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x_\varepsilon,S_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\longrightarrow\infty\] as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Thus small stationarity residual alone gives no uniform distance-to-solution control across this family; an error bound with controlled modulus is additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the scaling parameter decreases to zero, scaled quadratics admit points whose stationarity residual vanishes while their distance from the unique solution diverges.
knowledge_statements.title: Small Residual Far from Solutions

children.title: Small Residual with Large Objective Gap
children.top_down_role: Failure of stationarity quality to control objective quality without additional structure.

assumptions_latex: The constrained residual is \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,f'(x)+N_C(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(x)\to0\) but \(f(x)-\min_C f\to\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary constrained smooth counterexample
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained smooth example separating first-order residual from objective quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize \(f(x)=\log(1+x)\) over \(C=[0,\infty)\). Since \(f\) is strictly increasing, the unique minimizer is \(x^*=0\) and \(f(x^*)=0\). For every \(x>0\), \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\), so \[r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,f'(x)+N_C(x))=\frac{1}{1+x}\longrightarrow0.\] Nevertheless, \[f(x)-f(x^*)=\log(1+x)\longrightarrow\infty.\] Hence a small stationarity residual does not control objective suboptimality without an appropriate residual-to-gap condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the nonnegative ray, the logarithm has vanishing derivative at infinity while its objective gap from the minimizer diverges.
knowledge_statements.title: Small Residual with Large Objective Gap

children.title: Convexification-Representation Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Information losses caused by convexification or nonunique problem representations.

children.title: Clarke Stationarity Without Directional Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Critical points accepted by convexified stationarity but rejected by sharper directional tests.

assumptions_latex: Directional stationarity means \(f'(\bar x;d)\ge0\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R\).
Clarke stationarity means \(0\in\partial^C f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial^C f(0)\) although \(f'(0;d)<0\) for every \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained locally Lipschitz example using the one-sided directional derivative.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=-|x|\). At \(\bar x=0\), the Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of the two limiting slopes: \[\partial^C f(0)=[-1,1].\] Consequently \(0\in\partial^C f(0)\), so \(0\) is Clarke stationary. However, the directional derivative exists in every direction and satisfies \[f'(0;d)=-|d|<0\qquad(d\ne0).\] Thus \(0\) fails directional stationarity, demonstrating that convexified Clarke stationarity can accept a point possessing strict descent directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin is Clarke stationary for the negative absolute value, yet every nonzero direction is a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Stationarity Without Directional Stationarity

children.title: Active-Piece Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Weakening caused by aggregating incompatible active pieces.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is represented as the pointwise minimum of two smooth active pieces.
A convexified active-gradient test uses the convex hull of all active gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convexified test contains \(0\), whereas the true directional derivative is negative in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-of-smooth-pieces example showing loss under active-gradient convexification.

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 Relationship Between Quasidifferential and Clarke Subdifferential p. 109
source_refs.source_title: Introduction to Nonsmooth Optimization: Theory, Practice and Software

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\), where \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\). At \(0\), both pieces are active and \[\{\nabla f_i(0):i\in I(0)\}=\{-1,1\},\qquad 0\in\operatorname{co}\{-1,1\}.\] A test retaining only the convexified aggregate therefore reports stationarity. Yet the actual directional derivative is \[f'(0;d)=\min\{d,-d\}=-|d|<0\qquad(d\ne0).\] Convex aggregation cancels gradients belonging to incompatible active selections and discards the directional information that exposes descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying the two active gradients of a minimum creates cancellation and hides strict descent in every direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Information Loss

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Changes in criticality caused by alternative composite, DC, penalty, or constraint representations.

assumptions_latex: DC criticality for \(f=g-h\) means \(\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\).
All DC components are proper finite convex functions on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same function is DC-critical at \(0\) under one decomposition but not under another.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC criticality example; the function is fixed while its convex decomposition changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the decomposition \(f=g_1-h_1\) with \(g_1(x)=x\) and \(h_1(x)=0\), one has \[\partial g_1(0)=\{1\},\qquad \partial h_1(0)=\{0\},\] so \(0\) is not DC-critical. The identical function also has the decomposition \(f=g_2-h_2\), where \(g_2(x)=x+|x|\) and \(h_2(x)=|x|\). Now \[\partial g_2(0)=[0,2],\qquad \partial h_2(0)=[-1,1],\] whose intersection is \([0,1]\). Thus decomposition-based DC criticality is representation-sensitive unless the certificate is strengthened or tied to a prescribed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same nonsmooth convex term to both sides of a DC decomposition can change whether a fixed point is declared critical.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Stationarity

children.title: Calculus-Regularity Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Certificate defects caused by unsupported generalized-derivative calculus or failed constraint regularity.

children.title: Subdifferential Calculus Failure
children.top_down_role: Incomplete or spurious stationarity produced by invalid calculus rules.

assumptions_latex: \(\partial\) denotes the limiting subdifferential.
The unqualified chain-rule expression is \(F'(\bar x)^*\partial g(F(\bar x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'(0)^*\partial g(F(0))=\{0\}\subsetneq\mathbb R=\partial(g\circ F)(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar chain-rule counterexample when a qualification condition is omitted.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Subdifferential Calculus and Related Topics p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(F(x)=x^2\), and let \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\). Then \(g\circ F=\delta_{\{0\}}\), hence \[\partial(g\circ F)(0)=\mathbb R.\] On the other hand, \(F'(0)=0\) and \(\partial g(0)=\mathbb R\), so the formal chain-rule expression gives \[F'(0)^*\partial g(F(0))=0\mathbb R=\{0\}.\] Therefore applying a chain-rule equality without its qualification condition loses valid subgradients and can produce an incomplete stationarity system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indicator composed with the squaring map, the unqualified chain rule returns only zero although the true subdifferential is the whole line.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Calculus Failure

children.title: Normal-Cone Calculus Failure
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between true feasible geometry and analytically assembled normals.

assumptions_latex: \(N_S\) denotes the limiting normal cone to a closed set \(S\subset\mathbb R^2\).
The intersection normal is assembled using the unqualified rule \(N_{C\cap D}=N_C+N_D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(0)+N_D(0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\subsetneq\mathbb R^2=N_{C\cap D}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection-normal counterexample at a tangential, nonqualified set intersection.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y):y\ge x^2\}\), \(D=\{(x,y):y\le0\}\), and \(\bar z=(0,0)\). Their intersection is the singleton \(C\cap D=\{\bar z\}\), so \[N_{C\cap D}(\bar z)=\mathbb R^2.\] Individually, \[N_C(\bar z)=\{(0,-a):a\ge0\},\qquad N_D(\bar z)=\{(0,b):b\ge0\},\] and therefore \(N_C(\bar z)+N_D(\bar z)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\). The unqualified intersection rule misses all horizontal normals and misrepresents the feasible geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets meet tangentially at one point; summing their individual normals misses horizontal normals of the singleton intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Calculus Failure

children.title: Abnormal-Multiplier Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of objective information when multiplier normalization fails.

assumptions_latex: The equality-constrained problem is interpreted through Fritz John multipliers \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\ne(0,0)\).
The objective multiplier satisfies \(\lambda_0\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every Fritz John multiplier has \(\lambda_0=0\), so no normalization to \(\lambda_0=1\) is possible.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary Fritz John degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth equality-constrained example exhibiting only abnormal Fritz John multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)=x\) subject to \(h(x)=x^2=0\). The feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a local minimizer. Fritz John stationarity requires nonzero \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\), with \(\lambda_0\ge0\), such that \[0=\lambda_0 f'(0)+\lambda h'(0)=\lambda_0.\] Hence every admissible multiplier has \(\lambda_0=0\), while any \(\lambda\ne0\) supplies an abnormal certificate. The objective gradient disappears from the condition, and normalization to a KKT multiplier with \(\lambda_0=1\) is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate equality constraint forces the objective multiplier to zero, leaving a certificate that contains no objective information.
knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal-Multiplier Failure

children.title: Computational Verifiability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Gaps between mathematically natural stationarity notions and certificates accessible to finite computation.

children.title: Intractable Subdifferential Distance
children.top_down_role: Difficulty of evaluating distance to nonconvex generalized subdifferentials.

assumptions_latex: \(S=\partial f(x)\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and possibly nonconvex.
Available computation produces candidate elements of \(S\) but no global separation oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A candidate \(v\in S\) certifies only \(\operatorname{dist}(0,S)\le\|v\|\), not a matching lower bound or exact distance.

notation.meaning: Generalized subdifferential at the test point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-level boundary for nonconvex generalized subdifferentials; no formal complexity class is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonconvex generalized subdifferential \(S=\partial f(x)\), evaluating the residual means solving the global problem \[r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,S)=\inf_{v\in S}\|v\|.\] Producing any computable \(v\in S\) yields the verifiable upper bound \(r(x)\le\|v\|\). It does not show that no other disconnected branch of \(S\) lies closer to the origin. Without an exact projection method, an exhaustive representation, or a valid lower-bounding oracle for \(S\), exact residual evaluation and certification of \(r(x)>\varepsilon\) remain unavailable from sampled candidates alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finding one subgradient bounds the residual from above, but a nonconvex subdifferential may contain an unseen branch closer to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Intractable Subdifferential Distance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upper-bound observation is correct, but the broader claims that exact evaluation and positive lower-bound certification are unavailable depend on a formal access or oracle model. No source is supplied to define or justify that computational boundary.

children.title: Sampling-Estimation False-Certificate Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Finite-sample or stochastic errors that imitate stationarity.

children.title: Sampling-Induced False Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Finite-sample fluctuations that make a nonstationary point appear stationary.

assumptions_latex: A component index \(I\) is sampled uniformly from \(\{1,2\}\).
The reported residual is \(\widehat r(x)=|f_I'(x)|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\widehat r(x)=0)=\tfrac12\) although the population residual equals \(1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-component sampling example with an exact zero false certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1(x)=0\), \(f_2(x)=2x\), and \(f(x)=\tfrac12(f_1(x)+f_2(x))=x\). The population stationarity residual is \[r(x)=|f'(x)|=1\] at every \(x\). If one component \(I\) is sampled uniformly and the certificate uses \(\widehat r(x)=|f_I'(x)|\), then \[\widehat r(x)=0\ \text{when }I=1,\qquad \widehat r(x)=2\ \text{when }I=2.\] Consequently sampling reports exact stationarity with probability \(1/2\), even though the population objective is nowhere stationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single sampled component can have zero derivative with positive probability even though the population derivative is nonzero everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Induced False Stationarity

children.title: Estimation-Bias False Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Systematic derivative or residual estimation errors that imitate a valid certificate.

assumptions_latex: The true objective is differentiable with \(f'(x)=1\).
The certificate uses the mean of a biased estimator \(G(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G(x)]=0\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic biased-estimator example isolating bias from sampling variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x\), so \(\partial f(x)=\{1\}\) and the true stationarity residual is \(1\) everywhere. Define the estimator \(G(x)=0\) deterministically. Its bias is \[b(x)=\mathbb E[G(x)]-f'(x)=-1,\] and the estimator-based residual is \(\widehat r(x)=|\mathbb E[G(x)]|=0\). Thus even averaging infinitely many observations cannot correct this false stationarity certificate: concentration removes variance around the biased mean but does not make that mean a valid element of the true subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biased estimator can average exactly to zero while the true gradient remains one, so additional samples cannot repair the false certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Estimation-Bias False Stationarity

children.title: Variance-Driven Certificate Instability
children.top_down_role: Certificate sensitivity caused by noisy or high-variance estimators.

assumptions_latex: The oracle noise \(Z\) takes values \(-1\) and \(1\) with equal probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unbiased one-sample certificate is \(0\) or \(2\sigma\) with equal probability, while the true residual is \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased two-point oracle example separating estimator correctness from certificate stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sigma x\), where \(\sigma>0\), and let \(G(x)=\sigma(1+Z)\), with \(\mathbb P(Z=-1)=\mathbb P(Z=1)=1/2\). The oracle is unbiased because \(\mathbb E[G(x)]=\sigma=f'(x)\), and the true residual is \(r(x)=\sigma\). Nevertheless, the one-sample certificate satisfies \[\widehat r(x)=|G(x)|=\begin{cases}0,&Z=-1,\\2\sigma,&Z=1.\end{cases}\] Hence identical points alternate between exact apparent stationarity and a residual twice the truth, solely because of estimator variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased two-point oracle reports either zero or twice the true residual, making a one-sample certificate unstable.
knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Driven Certificate Instability

children.title: False-Certificate Detection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Statistical regimes limiting reliable separation of genuine stationarity from estimation artifacts.

assumptions_latex: \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\) is the population stationarity residual and \(\widehat r_N(x)\) is its sample-based estimate.
For prescribed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), an error bound \(\eta_N\ge 0\) satisfies \(\mathbb P\{\lvert \widehat r_N(x)-r(x)\rvert\le \eta_N\}\ge 1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat r_N(x)\le \varepsilon\) certifies only \(r(x)\le \varepsilon+\eta_N\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Residual estimated from a sample of size N.

review_flags: No supplied source directly supports the statistical detection boundary.
A source specifying sampling assumptions and a concentration or uniform-estimation bound is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise probabilistic boundary for interpreting a sample-estimated stationarity residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the event \(\lvert \widehat r_N(x)-r(x)\rvert\le \eta_N\), the triangle inequality gives \(r(x)\le \widehat r_N(x)+\eta_N\). Hence acceptance of \(x\) under the empirical test \(\widehat r_N(x)\le\varepsilon\) yields only the population certificate \(r(x)\le\varepsilon+\eta_N\). Without a valid bound \(\eta_N\), or another assumption linking the sampled and population residuals, an arbitrarily small value of \(\widehat r_N(x)\) does not logically exclude \(r(x)>\varepsilon\); the empirical test may therefore produce false stationarity certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampled residual detects population stationarity only up to its valid estimation-error radius; without such a bound, a small empirical residual can be a false certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: False-Certificate Detection Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and pointwise implication are mathematically coherent, but no source supports the sampling model or valid error radius. The statement also contains a triangle-inequality derivation that should be removed when sourced.

children.title: Inexact-Subproblem Certificate Contamination
children.top_down_role: Failure to separate inner solution error from outer stationarity residual.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable, \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper closed convex, and \(\lambda>0\).
\(T_\lambda(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(x-\lambda\nabla f(x))\), while an inner solver returns \(z\) satisfying \(\lVert z-T_\lambda(x)\rVert\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde r_\lambda(x)\le\varepsilon\) implies \(r_\lambda(x)\le\varepsilon+\delta/\lambda\), not generally \(r_\lambda(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Residual computed using the inexact inner solution.
Certified norm error of the inner solution.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the quantitative separation of inner and outer residual errors.
A proximal-algorithm source with an inexact subproblem criterion is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive contamination bound for an inexact proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reverse triangle inequality yields \(\lvert \widetilde r_\lambda(x)-r_\lambda(x)\rvert\le \lambda^{-1}\lVert z-T_\lambda(x)\rVert\le\delta/\lambda\). Consequently, a stopping test \(\widetilde r_\lambda(x)\le\varepsilon\) certifies at most \(r_\lambda(x)\le\varepsilon+\delta/\lambda\). Reporting \(\widetilde r_\lambda(x)\) as an outer stationarity residual without separately reporting or controlling \(\delta\) contaminates the certificate. In particular, the computed residual can approach zero while the exact residual remains as large as the unaccounted term \(\delta/\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact proximal solution adds at most its norm error divided by the stepsize to the outer residual, so the two errors must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Subproblem Certificate Contamination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive contamination bound fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but the quantitative inexact-subproblem criterion has no cited source. The statement also includes proof text.

children.title: Scaling-Sensitive Certificates
children.top_down_role: Distortion of residual magnitudes under objective, constraint, or coordinate scaling.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(r_f(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\).
\(\alpha>0\), and \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is invertible with \(x=Dy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective and coordinate rescaling change the numerical residual according to \(r_{\alpha f}(x)=\alpha r_f(x)\) and \(\sigma_{\min}(D)r_f(Dy)\le r_{f\circ D}(y)\le\lVert D\rVert r_f(Dy)\).
review_flags: No supplied source directly supports the stated subdifferential scaling identities.
A convex-analysis source for scalar and linear subdifferential chain rules is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of convex subdifferential-distance certificates to objective and coordinate scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Positive homogeneity of the convex subdifferential gives \(\partial(\alpha f)(x)=\alpha\partial f(x)\), and therefore \(r_{\alpha f}(x)=\alpha r_f(x)\). For the coordinate change \(x=Dy\), the invertible linear-chain rule gives \(\partial(f\circ D)(y)=D^{\mathsf T}\partial f(Dy)\). Hence \(\sigma_{\min}(D)r_f(Dy)\le r_{f\circ D}(y)\le\lVert D\rVert r_f(Dy)\). Thus zero residual is invariant under these rescalings, but any positive numerical tolerance is not; certificates from differently scaled formulations are incomparable unless their scaling factors are accounted for.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero stationarity is scaling-invariant, but residual magnitudes scale with the objective and are distorted by the singular values of a coordinate transformation.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Sensitive Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly targets scaling sensitivity, but the scalar and invertible-linear subdifferential rules and resulting singular-value bounds lack a source. The statement includes derivational proof text.

children.title: Fixed-Point Residual Interface
children.top_down_role: Residual certificates associated with projection, resolvent, and fixed-point reformulations.

assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is maximally monotone, \(B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is single-valued, and \(\lambda>0\).
\(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is the resolvent of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\lambda(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in A(x)+B(x)\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the maximally monotone operator A.

review_flags: The supplied fixed-point locator does not explicitly identify the resolvent inclusion equivalence.
A monotone-operator source with the forward-backward residual formula is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-backward resolvent representation of a monotone inclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(T_\lambda(x)=J_{\lambda A}(x-\lambda B(x))\) and \(R_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-T_\lambda(x))\). By the defining relation of the resolvent, \(x=T_\lambda(x)\) is equivalent to \(x-\lambda B(x)\in x+\lambda A(x)\), which is equivalent to \(0\in A(x)+B(x)\). Therefore \(R_\lambda(x)=0\) exactly characterizes solutions of the inclusion, while \(\lVert R_\lambda(x)\rVert\) supplies a computable fixed-point residual certificate whose numerical interpretation depends on \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward-backward fixed point is exactly a zero of the underlying monotone inclusion, and its scaled displacement supplies a computable residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residual Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Merit-Function Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural-residual merit representation for nonlinear complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the natural residual \(H(x)=x-\Pi_K(x-F(x))\) and the scalar merit function \(\Psi(x)=\tfrac12\lVert H(x)\rVert^2\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\Psi(x)\ge0\), and \(\Psi(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(x_iF_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Thus the zero set of \(\Psi\) is exactly the solution set of the nonlinear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared norm of the natural complementarity residual is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at nonlinear complementarity solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuous and \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\).
\(H(x)=x-\Pi_K(x-F(x))\), where \(\Pi_K\) is Euclidean projection onto \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Function Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized gap representation for a finite-dimensional variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in K\), the regularized gap function \(G_c(x)=\max_{y\in K}\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\tfrac c2\lVert x-y\rVert^2\}\) is nonnegative. Moreover, \(G_c(x)=0\) if and only if \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in K\). Thus the zero set of \(G_c\) is exactly the solution set of the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized gap is nonnegative on the feasible set and vanishes exactly at solutions of the variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\); and \(c>0\).
For \(x\in K\), \(G_c(x)=\max_{y\in K}\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\tfrac c2\lVert x-y\rVert^2\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_c(x)\ge0\), and \(G_c(x)=0\) if and only if \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in K\).
